newsitem.title: FRANCE: French court halts Yquem sale to LVMH - paper.
newsitem.headline: French court halts Yquem sale to LVMH - paper.

text.p: Count Alexandre de Lur-Saluces has won the first round in his fight to block the sale of the Chateau d'Yquem vineyard to luxury goods group LVMH, the newspaper Liberation reported on Thursday.

It said a court in Bordeaux halted the acquisition process and rejected LVMH's request for the appointment of a temporary manager for the property, which produces acclaimed Sauternes wines and has been owned by the Lur-Saluces family since 1785.
LVMH officials were not immediately available for comment.
The group announced last November that it had struck an agreement with the Marquis Eugene de Lur-Saluces, Alexandre's brother, and some 30 other family members to acquire 55 percent.

LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault said last week, during a presentation of the group's 1996 results, that LVMH was 55 percent owner of the company that owns the Chateau d'Yquem brand, stocks and vineyards and had a deal to acquire a majority of a second company that operates the vineyard.
He said he had made repeated overtures to Alexandre de Lur-Saluces and invited him to stay on to manage the property, but Lur-Saluces had refused even to see him.

"Yquem should not be relegated to the ranks of banal products," Lur-Saluces was quoted as saying in Liberation. He said LVMH's logic was incompatible with Chateau d'Yquem's longstanding objective to produce an exceptional wine.

D"Yquem, long regarded as the world's finest sweet after-dinner wine, is made from grapes that are left on the vine until they literally rot, concentrating the sugar. The grapes are then picked off by hand. In bad years, no wine is produced.

Lur-Saluces has argued that the sale announced in November was void because of a clause requiring the brothers' joint approval for the sale of the company which owns the rights to manage the property.
